turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response: Well, Dr. Smith, it's... it's a lot of things, really, but I suppose if I had to boil it down, I just don't feel like myself anymore. I mean, I've been working as a janitor over at the community college for going on fifteen years now, and usually, I'm the kind of guy who says hello to everyone in the halls, you know? I'd chat with the professors, the students, even the delivery guys. But lately, I just... I barely talk to anyone. I don't want to. It's like I just go completely flat and quiet inside. People will say good morning, and I just kind of stare at them, or I mumble something and walk away. I don't have the energy for it. And it's not just the talking. Just doing the job itself... getting started on my cleaning route every evening feels like I'm trying to push a loaded supply cart up a steep hill in the mud. I just stand there looking at the mop bucket and the trash bags, and I can't seem to make my arms and legs do what they're supposed to do. It takes everything I have just to put one foot in front of the other, and even then, I feel like I'm moving in slow motion. I used to take pride in getting the floors to shine, but now, I just don't care, and I don't have the drive to even try. It's just... it's all so heavy, Doctor. Everything is just so heavy and empty all at once.

turns.doctor_question: Have you been seeing or hearing things that others around you do not seem to notice?
turns.patient_response:
Well, it's funny you ask that, Doctor, because... well, actually it's not funny at all, it's been really throwing me off on top of everything else. You see, I work the evening shift, right? So by the time I get to the main corridors, especially over in the older buildings on campus, most of the students and the faculty are long gone. It gets real quiet in there. Usually it's just the hum of the vending machines and the squeak of my shoes on the linoleum. 

But lately... I’ll be out there mopping after hours. Just pushing the mop, trying to get through the night like I was telling you, feeling like I'm dragging a hundred pounds. And right when I'm near the main stairwell—the one with the heavy double doors—I'll hear this voice. It’s a man’s voice, real deep, and it is just as clear as you and me talking right now. He'll say my name. Just out of nowhere. Or sometimes he'll tell me I've missed a spot. 

I swear to you, it sounds like he is standing right there by the stairwell, just watching me work. The first time it happened, I actually stopped and leaned on my mop handle and called out, because I figured it was the night security guard making his rounds, or maybe a professor who stayed late to grade papers. I walked right over to the stairwell, and I pulled the door open, and I looked up and down the steps... and there was nobody. Not a single soul. 

And it just keeps happening. I'll be totally alone, the exterior doors are all locked, I know for an absolute fact I'm the only one in that wing of the building, and I'll hear him again. "You missed a spot." It really gives me a fright, you know? I just stand there holding the mop, staring at the empty space, and my heart starts pounding. I try to tell myself maybe it's just the acoustics of the building, because it does echo in those old halls, sure, but an echo has to come from somewhere, right? It has to be a real person making the noise to begin with. But when I look, there is never, ever anybody there. I just don't understand it.

symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient describes hearing a clear, deep man's voice speaking to them when they are completely alone, confirming auditory hallucinations.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever experienced these voices or felt this heavy, empty state during times in your life when you were not feeling this deeply depressed?
turns.patient_response:
Well, that's... that's an interesting question, Dr. Smith, because I've thought about that myself. You know, trying to make sense of it all. I keep a little calendar in my locker at work—just one of those free ones you get from the bank—and I try to mark down when things are really bad, just so I can keep track. And there was a time, not too long ago, maybe a couple of months back, where that heavy feeling... that feeling like I was walking through wet cement all the time, it actually lifted a bit. It wasn't perfect, I wasn't doing cartwheels down the hallway or anything, but for a stretch of, oh, maybe three or four weeks, I was actually getting through my shifts without feeling completely exhausted. I was eating my dinner—usually I just bring a turkey sandwich and an apple, maybe some potato chips if they're on sale—and I was actually finishing it, instead of just staring at it and throwing it in the breakroom trash. I felt... well, I felt a little more like myself. 

But the thing is, Doctor, even during those weeks when my mood was better and I had a little more energy, the other stuff didn't stop. I still heard that voice. I'd be sweeping near the stairwell, feeling okay, maybe even humming a little tune to myself, and clear as day, "You missed a spot," or he'd just say my name. "Gary." Just like that. And I still knew—I mean, I was absolutely convinced—that the security cameras in the hallways were tracking me. We have these little dome cameras, they put them in about five years ago, and I swear they follow me. I’ll move from the water fountain to the supply closet, and I can feel the lens shifting. Even when I was feeling pretty decent, eating my sandwiches, pushing the cart without feeling like I was dying, I still knew those cameras were watching my every move, and I still heard that man in the stairwell. So, yes, it seems like even when the darkness backs off a little, those other things... they just stay right there with me. It’s very unsettling, to tell you the truth, because you'd think if you felt better, everything would get better, right? But it just doesn't seem to work that way for me.

But looking back at the dates I circled—because I use a red pen for the really strange days, just a standard red ballpoint I found left behind in one of the lecture halls, I always keep it right there in my shirt pocket—I've been tracking it pretty closely. 

If I trace it all the way back to the very first time I heard that deep voice by the heavy double doors, and when I first started noticing the lenses on those dome cameras shifting to track my supply cart... it’s been about eleven months now. Eleven whole months of this. I remember specifically because it started right around the time we were doing the mid-semester deep cleans last year, and I had to order a whole new batch of floor wax from the supplier. I actually thought maybe the fumes from the floor stripper were getting to my head at first, you know? Because we have to use the industrial grade stuff for the scuff marks the kids leave. But the stripping and waxing only lasted a week, and the voice... well, the voice and the cameras just kept right on going. Every single month, right through the holidays, right through the spring, and here we are now, eleven months later, and he's still telling me I missed a spot. It's just exhausting, Doctor, carrying that around for nearly a whole year. You'd think a person would get used to it after all that time, but you really don't. turns.patient_response:
Well, if I really sit down and think about it... and I do think about it a lot, especially when I'm just sitting in the breakroom staring at the wall instead of eating my sandwich... I'd have to say the heavy periods are definitely the rule, not the exception. 

You see, ever since the move—I had to pack up and move into this smaller apartment across town right around the time all this started eleven months ago, which was just a tremendous hassle, hauling all those boxes by myself with my bad knees—but for most of the time since that move, it's just been this constant weight. The sadness, the low energy... it's just always there. And the guilt, too. I feel this awful guilt that I can't just snap out of it and be a normal, productive person, you know? I used to love tinkering with old radios on my days off, fixing up the wiring, listening to the static clear up. But I've had this complete loss of interest in all of it. And the really frustrating part, Dr. Smith, the thing that really wears a man down, is that it never really goes away. Even on the days when that deep voice in the stairwell is just relentless, or when my worries about those dome cameras watching me are the absolute main thing on my mind—like when I'm so focused on the lenses tracking my supply cart that my hands are actually sweating on the mop handle—even then, the sadness and that drained, empty feeling are still right there in the background. 

You'd think being terrified of someone watching you would kind of snap you out of being depressed, wouldn't you? Like adrenaline or something would take over. But it doesn't work like that. It’s like a heavy, wet blanket underneath everything else. It really never gives me a break.
